I regret however that, in the redistribution act which was passed last year, the powers that be saw fit to remove from that riding four of the best townships in the county. In my opinion this should never have been done. I do not believe in breaking county boundaries. When the next redistribution takes place, if I have any hand in it, those townships will be returned to Wentworth riding. I feel that the next riding of Wentworth should be more of a truly rural riding; and if I have anything to do with the matter it will be. I think it is only fair to the farmers in that riding that it should be so. Any change that was made this time should have been in that direction.
I wish for a few moments to refer to the serious erosion that has taken place along the shores of the great lakes, and particularly that portion of lake Ontario stretching from Hamilton to Niagara-on-the-Lake; that is along a great deal of the riding which I represent.
At a meeting held in Toronto in March of last year at the lake shore erosion conference the following resolution was passed:
Resolved that this organization ask the provincial and federal governments to instruct their engineers to make a survey of the erosion on the great lakes and report with a recommendation for a remedy; and in this report be included a report on the effects of the Ogoki and Albany river diversions on the level of the great lakes.
While this resolution went forward at that time, I doubt very much if the federal government has done anything about it, but I intend to find out.
A few years ago a former premier of Ontario approached the federal government and persuaded it to legalize diversion of the Ogoki and Albany rivers into the great lakes system, which means that while the present diversion at Chicago of the great lakes system is 3,500 cubic feet per second, there is now pouring in from northern Ontario water to

the extent of 5,200 cubic feet per second from the Albany river watershed. This means that we are getting an additional 1,700 cubic feet per second that should be flowing towards James bay and the Arctic circle.
It is argued by many engineers that this large additional volume which does not belong to the St. Lawrence watershed is one of the causes for the cycle of high levels that we have been experiencing on lakes Huron, Erie and Ontario; and it is easy to see that these lake levels, which are abnormally high when lashed by winds and storms, do most certainly erode the shore line of the lower lakes.
As I have said before, if the federal government does not do something soon, it will not be many years before that great Niagara fruit belt-possibly the greatest stone-fruit belt in Canada-will be wiped out altogether.
Taxes must be reduced. I feel that two of the first to go should be the sales tax and the 25 per cent luxury tax. They are both hampering trade; they are an aggravation; and the sales tax especially is one that is borne by those who are least able to afford it. It does not concern me one bit when this tax was imposed or who imposed it. I consider it is wrong. We should never have had it except, perhaps, as a war measure, and it should be removed. In some cases, of course, the tax has been removed. But one matter that I feel is misleading is this. While the 8 per cent sales tax has been removed from certain foodstuffs, the ingredients of packaged - foods are still subject to it; so that while the 8 per cent tax has been removed from the finished product, as a result of the retention of sales tax on spices, pectins and other commodities that go into the processing of soups, jams, et cetera, there will be no noticeable reduction in the price of these foods.
One tax that I feel should most certainly be removed is that on soft drinks. While I realize that practically 90 per cent of the soft-drink bottling plants in Canada are privately-owned, that by far the greater proportion of them are small plants with small distribution, and that many of these plants which employ a great many people are finding it hard to make ends meet, it is certainly a situation which should be altered immediately. Far more important to my mind, however, is the consideration that the kiddies should get back their five-cent drinks and chocolate bars.
One matter with which I most certainly am not satisfied is the attitude of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) and of the government with respect to a house committee being set up to deal with veterans affairs. The minister was questioned some
The Address-Mr. Lennard days ago in the house and he said quite definitely that, in the opinion of the government, it was not necessary to have a committee on veterans affairs this session. This, in my opinion, is most certainly neglect on the part of the government and a let-down to the veterans of this country. The Red Cross girls, the St. John's ambulance brigade and several other groups who served in the second great war most certainly did not get what was due them. The British Canadians who have lived for twenty continuous years in Canada and are veterans of the first great war are, in my opinion, most certainly entitled to war veterans allowance. I might say that the Minister of Veterans Affairs, during the discussion on the estimates towards the end of last session, said that he was still studying that problem, and was still considering the matter of making some allowance to the British Canadian veterans. But as yet we have heard nothing in that respect. I think the war veterans allowance should be granted to them. I do not know why it was not done years ago.
This war veterans committee of the House of Commons should be a permanent committee. It should be a standing committee which should meet every session and not just every two years when it coincides with the annual meeting of the Canadian Legion and whenever possible manages to wind up its deliberations shortly before the annual meeting when there is generally a great round of back-slapping. The veterans affairs committee of the House of Commons should meet every session if only to consider in detail the estimates of the department. Since I have mentioned that, I think there should be a standing committee for every department of government. These standing committees should consider the estimates in committee. The work would be done more thoroughly, and it would save a great deal of time which is now wasted in the House of Commons.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I would speak for about fifteen minutes. I think it was Mark Twain who once said that if a man could not say all he knew about any one subject in twenty minutes he should not have the privilege of saying anything; but I have covered a lot of ground and I am still staying within the limit. As a matter of fact, I am just about as much fed up with these long-winded speeches in the House of Commons as anyone else.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I thoroughly agree with thoughts expressed at the recent national Liberal convention
which was held in Ottawa on August 5, 6 and 7, 1948, to the effect that it was about time that this country got back to responsible
1288	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Stanfield government. It is about time, and it is long overdue, that this country returned to parliamentary government, with the people's elected representatives having a say as to what should be done. It is about time the bureaucrats were put in their places. There is a great deal wrong with the present system that cannot be blamed upon any government in particular, but the last two governments have gone a very long way to bring about the present situation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hardly know just why I am on my feet. I am not much of a talker anyway, and I am never exactly sure what I should or should not do since I came to this place; therefore my position tonight is nothing very new.
I should like to congratulate the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown). I have a great deal of admiration for that hon. member and I certainly wish him every success in his political career.
I do not know the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Demers); I have not had the pleasure of meeting him, but he made a fine speech and I wish him every success in his political life.
The first matter on which I should like to speak for a few minutes is pensions for blind people, cripples and people who are permanently invalided. I know that today we have pensions for the blind, but these pensions should be a great deal higher than they are. Blindness is a terrible affliction. I believe that a blind person should get a pension even though he has the means of making a living and perhaps owns a little property. Just because he has a little bit of this world's goods in the form of property, and possibly a small income, that does not mean that he should be deprived of a pension. I believe that the pension should be twice as large as it is today.
As for our cripples and invalids, I could never understand why some consideration was not given to these poor unfortunate people. There are hundreds of them in every province of this dominion. Some of them have not a cent that they can call their own. They are dependent on their relatives or on some person who will keep them. These unfortunate people should be given some kind of a pension so that they can have a ltitle money which they can at least call their own. I believe that the only reason why these people have never received any great consideration is that they have no great political influence. Today, regardless of party, anybody who has not much political influence never receives a great deal of attention.


The next matter to which I should like to refer is the conservation of our forests. The forests are by far the greatest form of wealth that this country has. We can all agree that our forests have been depleted far too rapidly. Only the other day I read in the paper that one of the ministers in British Columbia said that the forests of that province were being depleted at a very rapid rate. I know that our forests in Nova Scotia, and in the maritime provinces generally, are going at a rapid rate and not much is being done about it. I do not see why the dominion government should not assume a great deal of responsibility for reforestation, or at least supplement the provinces by giving them grants to help reforestation and to guard against fires and insects. Fires and insects are just as heavy a drain on our forests as cutting operations. I know that in our province the birch is all gone. Many people thought that birch was good only for making furniture or for cutting up into firewood, or something of that kind; but in New Hampshire and Vermont I believe they are using birch and the other hardwood trees for making pulp.
It is pretty hard to place the value on our forests for future generations. The future wealth of this country will greatly depend on the conservation of our forests, and I do believe that the dominion government would be wise to do everything they can to give grants to the provinces, or set up areas themselves for reforestation, and do everything they can to protect our forests.
It may be said that this all takes money, and it might be asked where we are to get it. I have a little suggestion to make. It may not meet with very much favour, but hon. members have read in the papers that the President of the United States formed a commission or a committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Hoover. That commission was to look into the consolidating of government departments in the United States with a view to bringing about greater efficiency in government and lessening the cost of administration. Mr. Hoover and his committee brought in a recommendation that would cut the cost of government in that country by about $2 billion. I know politics well enough to know that that whole $2 billion could never be saved. I think perhaps we should set up a committee to inquire into the cost of government with a view to cutting down the cost of doing the business of the country, at the same time doing it more efficiently and making it much easier for the ministers. It could run into a very large figure. It would also be a great help toward getting a cut in income tax.

May I say a word about income tax? Take a married man with two children, and calculate what income tax he has to pay this year and what he has paid back to 1940. It is pretty hard to see how he has been able to get along as well as he has. Take the great middle-class people of this country. Take the people who have incomes of from $5,000 to $25,000. The chap above that can get along all right. If he cannot, it is his own hard luck. The people on incomes of $5,000 to $25,000 are the great middle class who are the very backbone of our country. I can well understand that our socialist friends to the left would very much like to get rid of the middle-class people; it is to their interests not to have too strong a middle class in this country. Our friends on the government benches across the way are doing the best they can to help the socialists along in that, so far as I can see.
I would ask that in his coming budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) give every possible relief to these people in the form of a substantial reduction in their income taxes, because, as I said before, they are the very backbone of any democratic country, no matter where it may be. If one does not find in a country a large and influential middle class, then that country does not amount to much.
I shall not spend much time discussing the tax on soft drinks. I would say however that any government, with a surplus of three-quarters of a billion dollars, which cannot afford to take off that two-cent tax on bottled soft drinks, and soda fountain drinks, has something wrong with it. This is a nuisance tax of the worst possible variety; certainly in my view we would be well rid of it.
The same observations could be applied to the tax on leather goods. First of all let me say that I have no connection whatever with the manufacture and sale of leather goods; but I do know that when a manufacturer has to add 35 per cent to his sale price of luggage and other leather goods he is faced with an unpleasant procedure. No one wishes to stock up at this time with merchandise bearing these heavy taxes. The result is that, with the tax applied, the manufacturer proceeds to cut down volume because he does not know just what is going to happen. In my view this is a most unfair tax applied only to leather goods. One such type of manufactured goods should not be singled out for such heavy tax action.
Much the same could be said with respect to jewelry. Of course the jeweler collects the tax of 25 per cent from the consumer. I
The Address-Mr. Stanfield believe even our socialist friends to the left would agree that today costume jewelry is more or less a necessity. The same would apply to many other articles sold by the jeweler. I should say that as we are getting back to a permanent peacetime basis many of these heavy taxes against certain types of businessmen, such as those engaged in the manufacture and sale of leather goods and in the production and sale of jewelry, might well be reduced or completely eliminated.
Perhaps in passing I might say something which I am sure will receive the support of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). I believe margarine should be given a distinctive colour, and that such colour should not be the same as that of butter. I believe further that margarine should carry a distinctive wrapping so that the product could not be associated with or sold to the public as butter. As the butter manufacturers and dairymen are not protected by any patents or trade-marks, I say the margarine manufacturer should not be permitted to have the advantage of packaging his product to resemble butter. In this I believe we would all agree.
When I resume my remarks, I should like to speak about conditions in the maritime provinces.
On motion of Mr. Stanfield the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when an hon. member is speaking other hon. members ought not to wander around, interfering and interrupting. I would ask to have them named.

Before the adjournment would
the Prime Minister indicate the next order of business after the vote has been taken on the debate on the speech from the throne?

There are several items
which are quite urgent. I should expect that the first of these to be dealt with would be the resumption of the debate on the motion of the Minister of Justice that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into a committee of the whole on a resolution providing for the introduction of a bill to continue certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.

Well then, without pressing the point too vigorously, may I take it that, unless

Business of the House there is some special reason, we may assume this will be debated following the completion of the vote on the motion to adopt the speech from the throne?
